Exploring Technologies is the ideal place to compare processes rather than rush toward one “best” machine. Keep each build small enough that students can investigate a user, communicate alternatives, fabricate safely, test evidence, and name what they would change.

## Project directions

:::: {.ter-project-grid}
::: {.ter-project-card}
### Personal work-zone organizer
<p class="ter-course-code">TIJ1O · Organizer family</p>
Design a stable home for three real classroom items so a user can identify, remove, and replace each item without lifting the organizer.
<dl><dt>Process</dt><dd>Cardboard mock-up → vector or CAD model → laser-cut, 3D-printed, or hand-built prototype</dd><dt>Skills</dt><dd>Measurement, alternatives, access clearance, labelling, user test</dd><dt>Difficulty / size</dt><dd>Introductory · about 250 × 180 × 150 mm</dd><dt>Material</dt><dd>Corrugated board first; plywood, sheet plastic, or filament only after testing</dd><dt>Structural</dt><dd>Wide base, low centre of mass, no wall mounting in the first iteration</dd><dt>Safety</dt><dd>Round exposed corners; keep cutting and hot-tool work under local supervision</dd><dt>Library</dt><dd><a href="../../../teaching-materials/laser-cutting/?technology=exploring-technologies&type=tool-holders">Measured holder starters</a></dd><dt>Lesson</dt><dd><a href="../../03-laser-cutting/06-tool-holder.qmd">Tool Holder</a></dd><dt>Extension</dt><dd>Adapt the same retention logic for a different technology area and compare criteria</dd></dl>
:::
::: {.ter-project-card}
### Technology-area comparison display
<p class="ter-course-code">TIJ1O · Display family</p>
Explain how one method, such as laser cutting or 3D printing, could solve different problems in four technology areas.
<dl><dt>Process</dt><dd>Research → thumbnail layouts → vector composition → stable tabletop display</dd><dt>Skills</dt><dd>Source evaluation, hierarchy, icons, typography, audience feedback</dd><dt>Difficulty / size</dt><dd>Introductory · two A4-equivalent panels</dd><dt>Material</dt><dd>Cardstock, reused corrugated board, or thin plywood</dd><dt>Structural</dt><dd>Stand must resist a light bump and remain readable at one metre</dd><dt>Safety</dt><dd>Use original or permitted imagery; verify machine-safe materials</dd><dt>Library</dt><dd><a href="../../../teaching-materials/laser-cutting/?technology=exploring-technologies&type=project-components">Display components</a></dd><dt>Lesson</dt><dd><a href="../../02-digital-design/04-layout-typography-colour.qmd">Layout, Type & Colour</a></dd><dt>Extension</dt><dd>Add an accessible digital version with alt text and strong contrast</dd></dl>
:::
::: {.ter-project-card}
### Measurement sampler
<p class="ter-course-code">TIJ1O · Gauge family</p>
Build a clearly labelled reference that measures one thing (length, angle, radius, hole size, or spacing) and demonstrate what it cannot certify.
<dl><dt>Process</dt><dd>Choose measurand → draw exact geometry → fabricate → compare with a trusted instrument</dd><dt>Skills</dt><dd>Units, datum selection, scale verification, error recording</dd><dt>Difficulty / size</dt><dd>Introductory · under 220 × 150 mm</dd><dt>Material</dt><dd>Card for layout trial; dimensionally stable sheet for final prototype</dd><dt>Structural</dt><dd>Protect fine features and include a hanging or storage feature</dd><dt>Safety</dt><dd>Classroom reference only, not an inspection-certified instrument</dd><dt>Library</dt><dd><a href="../../../teaching-materials/laser-cutting/?technology=exploring-technologies&type=jigs-gauges">Jigs and gauges</a></dd><dt>Lesson</dt><dd><a href="../../03-laser-cutting/03-measure-place.qmd">Measure + Place</a></dd><dt>Extension</dt><dd>Quantify kerf or shrinkage and revise the source file</dd></dl>
:::
::::

## Teaching and assessment notes

Assess the evidence trail: user need, two alternatives, labelled dimensions, safe process choice, test result, and next iteration. A polished object without that evidence is not stronger than a rough prototype that teaches the student something specific.

::: {.ter-curriculum-relevance}
**Curriculum context:** These projects suit broad TIJ1O exploration because students encounter design, communication, measurement, materials, tools, systems, safety, and careers without treating any single shop as the definition of Technological Education.
:::
